In summary, we expect the iPhone 18 Pro won't bring major upgrades over its predecessor. In fact, if you're using an older iPhone right now, there are plenty of reasons to pick up an iPhone 17 Pro before the new model launches next week.

Among the relatively few anticipated upgrades, the biggest headline on paper is the variable aperture on the main camera. But in actual use, will this change really make a noticeable difference...?

Variable Aperture and Depth of Field Control

One of the biggest differences between photos taken with a DSLR or mirrorless camera and those shot with an iPhone is the control over depth of field.

With traditional cameras, a wide aperture can create shallow depth of field, and its most common use is separating the subject from the background. Portrait photos are the classic example (which is why Apple's simulated shallow depth-of-field effect is called "Portrait Mode").

Conversely, when shooting landscapes or cityscapes, a narrow aperture is typically used to keep everything from the foreground to the background sharp and clear.

So variable aperture has always been a standard feature on any traditional lens. By comparison, iPhones have always used fixed-aperture lenses. (There are actually a few ways to achieve shallow depth of field on iPhone, and I'll write a separate article about that once the new model arrives, but these are exceptions rather than the norm.)

Variable Aperture Coming to iPhone Lenses

We expect this year's iPhone to be among the first models equipped with a variable-aperture lens. It's still unclear whether this feature will apply to both iPhone 18 Pro models, or be limited to the Pro Max only. Either way, it's expected to be limited to the main lens, not the ultrawide or telephoto.

On paper this is indeed big news. In theory, a variable-aperture lens would let us control depth of field. But in practice, we shouldn't get too excited about the effect shown in the main image at the top of the article—the reason is that some things simply won't change.

The Bad News

The main limiting factor for iPhone isn't the lens aperture (the aperture itself is already quite large), but the size of the image sensor. All else being equal, the larger the sensor, the more pronounced the shallow depth-of-field effect can be. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhone sensors are much smaller, and that's not going to change this year.

With the same sensor size and an aperture that's only marginally wider, according to the laws of physics we shouldn't expect a dramatic difference.

The Possibly Good News

That said, there may still be a glimmer of hope. Adding a mechanical variable aperture inside an iPhone lens is by no means a simple engineering feat. Given the compact size of the lens, this design is complex and expensive.

So the question we have to ask is: why would Apple spend so much effort and money on something with such modest expected benefits? If the end result is just that calculated degree of difference, it simply wouldn't be worth doing.

This makes me wonder—if Apple really plans to list this new feature as a major selling point, there must be something else behind it.

One possibility I can think of is that this optical upgrade is almost a cover for a major improvement to Portrait Mode. The simulated effect has been getting better year by year, but there's still room for improvement—or perhaps through the AI computing power of an upgraded chip, Apple could achieve a more natural-looking result?

If that's the case, I think most people wouldn't mind this kind of "shortcut"—the benefits brought by the variable aperture aren't that significant; rather, it's the software improvements that are key to delivering a more meaningful upgrade. For most people, what matters most is the final result. That's my best guess for now.

Got a better idea? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
